evidence: Lewis & Short s.v. rēs: “a matter, affair, event, fact, circumstance, occurrence”
terms.comment: Latin has no everyday word for a phenomenon: it says rēs with an adjective or a clause (rēs nova, rēs mīra, quod fit), or names the thing itself.

evidence: Cic. Rep. 1.15: nūllum esse prōdigium, of an eclipse of the moon (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Only for an extraordinary event taken as a sign from the gods, or a monstrous thing; Cicero insists that an eclipse is not one.

evidence: Lact. Inst. 2.5.11 (plural, of appearances in the sky) (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The Greek word, rare in Latin: Phaenomena is the title of Aratus’ poem on the stars (Lewis & Short). Morgan–Owens prefers it as the more precise term for something perceived by the senses.

sources: Lewis & Short: res · Lewis & Short: prodigium · Lewis & Short: phaenomenon
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. phenomenon.
